The post Book Review: The World Atlas of Wine (9th Edition) appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
The ninth iteration of the World Atlas of Wine is, first and most urgently, heavy. Anyone north of a certain age will recognize it immediately as both a coffee table book and an unsolicited personal trainer. Anyone living alone and worrying about home security will take comfort in its alternate use as a deterrent. It is, like so many other things in 2026 hustle culture, doing more than one job.

The authorship is, as wine credentials go, essentially a Supreme Court: Hugh Johnson and Jancis Robinson, two names so established in the field that introducing them feels slightly presumptuous, joined this time around by Julia Harding, who is herself no one’s idea of a lightweight: intellectually or, one assumes, physically after carrying the manuscripts for this book around for any length of time. This is the ninth edition of an atlas that first appeared in 1971, when the wine world looked substantially different and nobody had yet coined the phrase “having a moment.”

If you’ve kept the faith through previous editions (the last one arrived in 2019), this volume rewards loyalty with the thoroughness of someone taking diligent notes in class for five years. Eighteen new maps, bringing the total to 240. Updated climate data. An expanded focus on North America. New photographs, new texts, new illustrations: eventually, the word “new” begins to lose function, as words do when you stare at them too long. However, in this case the repetition is well-earned: there is genuinely a great deal of new here, and all of it is quite good.

What hasn’t changed with this atlas is its density and intensity, which is considerable, and may cause some newcomers to regard the thing the way a first-year law student regards a casebook: a blend of awe, anxiety, and a tinge of anxiety that they may have purchased the wrong book. To those people, I would say: you have not, and apply gentle pressure on your brakes. This is not a book written the intent to be read cover-to-cover, or even finished. It was written for repeated visits, with a glass of something you’re still figuring out, across years and seasons and the gradual accumulation of opinions and preferences. The next edition won’t arrive for a while, so there is no urgency here. There is only wine, time, and section after section that will teach you things you didn’t know you wanted to know.

It is a reference guide, scholarly work, and a genuinely enjoyable read: three things that don’t often coexist in a singular volume. Indispensable is a word that may be selected when running out of compelling word choices, but in this case, it applies with accuracy and precision. There is simply nothing else quite like it, which, for a ninth edition published across five decades, is a remarkable achievement. It is also a tremendous amount of pressure on anyone selected for the tenth edition.

A / $75 [BUY IT NOW FROM AMAZON]

title: Review: Skeeter’s Nootkatone Flavored Whiskey
summary:

The post Review: Skeeter’s Nootkatone Flavored Whiskey appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Tamworth Distilling is well known for some crazy spirits — crab-flavored whiskey, anyone? — but its latest innovation might be it’s most bizarre yet. To understand it, first you must understand what nootkatone is. I’d never heard of it, but it turns out in some parts of the world, nootkatone is used as a natural mosquito repellant used in lieu of chemicals. It’s a naturally occurring compound found in grapefruit peel and Alaska yellow cedar, and it’s commonly applied as a spray or balm.

For Tamworth, it’s also a flavoring that can be used with whiskey, though you’re not necessarily intended to drink it straight. Much like a nootkatone product designed for use on the body, Skeeter’s Nootkatone Whiskey (build on top of a 60% abv base of blended whiskey) comes in a spray bottle, designed to be spritzed across the top of your drink — whatever it might be. The flavor of nootkatone is infused into your beverage, while presumably also helping to keep mosquitos away from you in the process.

Skeeter’s Nootkatone Flavored Whiskey Review

Compared to a spraydown of OFF!, Skeeter’s Nootkatone is awfully mild. I sprayed five spritzes into an empty glass and could barely smell anything — just a vaguely fruity and more clearly piney character emerging from the tumbler. Spritzing into a tighter-mouthed Glencairn helped focus some of those aromas, again coming across with notes of evergreen and a spicier lemongrass note. For my nose, the grapefruit notes played second fiddle, though they become more dominant the longer you let them linger in glass.

With some whiskey, the aromas become much stronger, right away, all of the above amplified considerably. The palate showcases those grapefruit notes quite clearly, turning minty as the whiskey develops. The fadeout easily connotes lemongrass and a heady pine-eucalyptus quality. But naturally, all of this will depend heavily on the cocktail or spirit to which you choose to apply Skeeter’s, how much of it you spray, and how concerned you are with being eaten alive while in the great outdoors. It’s a curious product — and not something I think needs a formal rating — but likely more useful as a conversation piece than a cocktail adjunct.

120 proof.

$24 (100ml)

title: Review: Canned Cocktails of Moth (Updated 2026)

The post Review: Canned Cocktails of Moth (Updated 2026) appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Moth — formally “MOTH:” with a colon — is relatively unknown in the U.S., but it’s actually the UK’s #1 premium ready-to-drink cocktail brand. Short for “Mix of Total Happiness,” Moth has at least 10 different flavors, with four available in the States in the form of a mixed four-pack, one 200ml can of each cocktail: Margarita, Espresso Martini, Mojito, and Piña Colada.

Each cocktail is made with premium ingredients — no malt liquor here — and comes as a single serving (or maybe two) that’s ready to drink when poured over ice. Moth even says you can sip them straight from the can, but we wouldn’t dream of it.

Update: Moth’s repertoire has been expanding of late. We’re enhancing our coverage with looks at additional products in the canned cocktail line. We’ll continue to update this roundup as new flavors arrive.

Moth Mojito – Made with rum from Duppy Share, mint, lime, and soda. This tastes about on point and as it should, though the lime shows off a bit of the same chemical/citric acid note that the margarita suffers from. Fortunately there’s more here (and a better spirit, perhaps) to temper it, alongside with a gentle sweetness that furthers the cause. The effervescence is very mild, as is the mint — perhaps the drink’s only real shortcoming. The lower abv actually works in favor of the drink, giving it a refreshing, citrus-driven quality that feels perfect for poolside. I’d definitely sample this one again. 10% abv. A-

Moth Pina Colada – Made with rum from Duppy Share, coconut liqueur, and pineapple. This isn’t the creamy concoction you might get on the beach — there’s no Coco Lopez here — but rather an on-the-rocks version that’s heavy on the pineapple. The coconut liqueur underneath is very sweet (what pina colada isn’t?), and there’s a gentle but present white rum character behind that, showing off a touch of funk. The finish leans heavier on the coconut, giving it that inevitable suntan lotion quality, though it never comes up short of being exuberantly tropical. I’d recommend serving this blended with ice, but that might defeat the purpose of the RTD presentation. Your call. 10% abv. A-

Moth Cosmopolitan – Vodka, triple sec, cranberry, and lime. Arguably the most authentic cocktail in the Moth collection, this tastes like it was made seconds ago and needs only a martini glass and a twist of lime peel to seal the deal. The cranberry and lime are tart, the triple sec offering a gentle sweetness in lieu any significant added sugar. The vodka (whatever is used here) offers no bite at all, the finish instead perking right up with a kick of orange. Keep a few cans on hand for when the lightweights come to visit. You may just want to pour one yourself. 14.9% abv. A-

Moth Espresso Martini – Made with vodka from Wood Brothers, coffee liqueur, and cold brew. Authentic but flat, note that you won’t get much froth from this unless you pour the drink out and shake it with ice; just shaking the can won’t do the trick. Either way, even without a creamy head, the cocktail offers a strong coffee aroma that entices, even though the palate comes across a bit on the mild side. A moderate to heavy sweetness is in part responsible for that, evoking thoughts of coconut nectar and, later, a significant fruity quality: raspberry and strawberry jam layered on with the finish. They gentle and pretty, the fruity qualities may be a bit overwhelming if you’re not on the mood and looking for a more straightforward, bittersweet (or chocolate-leaning) flavor. 14.9% abv. B+

Moth Spicy Margarita – The spicy version (adding chili to the recipe) of the below margarita is an improvement, tempering the lime considerably and letting the tequila do more of the work. Yes, there’s still plenty of citrus evident, especially on the biting nose, but the palate tempers it enough to evoke the flavor of a freshly made margarita. Oddly, the spice is virtually nonexistent: The heat is extremely gentle,  offering just a mild touch of pepper on the lips. Nonetheless, it works. More than anything, it serves to amplify the underlying tequila, which is lightly vegetal and green, but which eventually fades into the background and gives way to triple sec and a gentler lime note on the finish. 14.9% abv. B+

Moth Margarita – Made with tequila from Enemigo, triple sec, and lime. Emphasis on the lime: This is weighed down with the fruit from the start, giving off a sharp, citric acid vibe that bites at the back of the mouth. A lot of ice helps it settle down, but this comes at the expense of the rest of the cocktail, which isn’t particularly powerful when it comes to the tequila component, especially. I drank most of the can, but it hit me closer to a stout glass of Sprite than I’d have liked. 14.9% abv. B

Moth Passionfruit Martini – Made with vodka, vanilla (or vanilla vodka), passion fruit, and peaches. This is Moth’s spin on the iconic Pornstar Martini, and if you’ve ever had that overwhelming libation, you’ll recognize an authentic recreation here. Vanilla is overwhelming at first, almost creating a coconut cream character it’s so sweet and sticky. Color aside, the vanilla overpowers the passion fruit, and the candylike combination ends up coming across as a bit chemical. You can taste the sugar-rush headache forming as you sip it, but it’s nonetheless a solid pick for ’90s night. 14.9% abv. B

$20 per four-pack of 200ml cans

title: Book Review: Hugh Johnson’s Pocket Wine Book 2027 (50th Anniversary Edition)
summary:
No matter how one chooses to frame it, a half-century of consistently doing anything well is both a remarkable feat and a noteworthy accomplishment. Yes, innumerable vineyards around the globe have been making wine for three to four times that length, but we’re not talking about them. Today, we celebrate Ol’ Hugh Johnson and his…

The post Book Review: Hugh Johnson’s Pocket Wine Book 2027 (50th Anniversary Edition) appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
No matter how one chooses to frame it, a half-century of consistently doing anything well is both a remarkable feat and a noteworthy accomplishment. Yes, innumerable vineyards around the globe have been making wine for three to four times that length, but we’re not talking about them. Today, we celebrate Ol’ Hugh Johnson and his pocket notebook, which started out as a Pocket Encyclopedia back in 1977, when Studio 54, Lambrusco and Star Wars were royalty and nothing bad was happening anywhere on planet Earth. Somehow, this feat of longevity has endured and morphed into appointment-reading for a few generations of wine experts and newcomers looking to level up a step or three in their wisdom.

The question of what to say about a book in its fiftieth year of publication is, frankly, a more interesting editorial dilemma than it might appear on the surface. You can’t approach it like a debut. You can’t review it as though it has something to prove because it doesn’t, and it knows it doesn’t. However, there is something about a reference guide carrying itself with exactly the right amount of earned gravitas. It does not present itself with pomposity or arrogance, but in the way a well-seasoned doctor wearing bifocals delivers a diagnosis: here is what we know to be true, here is what it means, here are your options. You are welcome.

What Johnson devised, and what he and Margaret Rand, the book’s editor and superhero doing a substantial amount of heavy lifting required to keep this thing current, continue to build every year, is a document with the central premise that wine is important enough to take seriously but enjoyable enough that taking it too seriously defeats the point of it all. Threading this needle is harder than it sounds. The wine world, as an institutional entity, prides itself on being more comfortable around the “too seriously” end of the spectrum, producing a great deal of writing that reads as though the author is not entirely sure you deserve to be drinking what you’re drinking. Johnson and Rand, for fifty years now, have written as though they are reasonably certain you do, one of many reasons people keep buying and recommending this book.

Somewhat surprisingly, the 2027 edition opens on a rather sober tone, marking not its golden jubilee with a victory lap but with an urgent and necessary supplement on wine and climate change. Specifically, how a rapidly shifting climate is remaking the way wine is grown, made and consumed, and what, if anything, can be done about it. Not a celebratory topic, but one with purpose, and the decision to spend this edition’s bonus pages on something important rather than something flowery and commemorative says something admirable about the book’s long-running commitment to usefulness over sentimentality. The half-century party favor is a homework assignment, which is on brand in the best possible way.

The core of the book is, as it has always been and will likely always be, a reference section featuring thousands of growers, producers, regions, and appellations, organized with the rigorous economy of something that has been refined across fifty iterations. The font is, as it has always been, small. Small in a way that has become part of the book’s personality. For those around the same age as this series or older, reading glasses are not optional, and there is zero shame in considering a magnifying glass. The book will not apologize for this, and well it shouldn’t, because the alternative of larger type would result in fewer facts and would be worse off for it.

As always, the Pocket Wine Book organizes the overwhelming complexity of the wine world into something functional and useful. Grape varieties are explained. Regions are mapped. Which vintages to cellar, and which to drink now. Which wines to leave alone for reasons that will eventually become clear. Which growers are worth paying attention to and, importantly, why. It’s not just the verdict but the reasoning behind it, offered in prose that respects reader intelligence without requiring a WSET Diploma.

For newcomers, the experience of opening this book can be overwhelming. It is roughly equivalent to walking into a library and realizing, with a mixture of excitement and vertigo, that you have underestimated the size of your research assignment. This is fine. The book is not going anywhere, nor is wine, and hopefully neither are you. Start somewhere interesting, follow the threads, and accept that knowledge will accumulate over years of regular consultation, not a single read-through. There are far worse habits to develop. For veterans, the 2027 update delivers what it always delivers: the world of wine as it actually exists right now, annotated by people who have been watching it carefully for a very long time, presented without fuss or excessive ceremony in something small enough to fit in a bookbag, though large enough in ambition to have outlasted, by a comfortable margin, nearly everything else in its category.

A / $20 [BUY IT NOW FROM AMAZON]

title: Review: Crown Royal 32 Years Old
summary:
Crown Royal‘s Extra Rare offerings have been getting older and older — how much well-aged whisky does this distillery have sitting around? — with the new high-water mark for the line now hitting 32 years of age. This expression comes in the snazziest, be-tassled velvet bag I’ve seen from the brand to date and is…

The post Review: Crown Royal 32 Years Old appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Crown Royal‘s Extra Rare offerings have been getting older and older — how much well-aged whisky does this distillery have sitting around? — with the new high-water mark for the line now hitting 32 years of age. This expression comes in the snazziest, be-tassled velvet bag I’ve seen from the brand to date and is in turn stored inside a gold cardboard box with double doors in front.

These extremely old Crown Royal expressions haven’t been overly dazzling in the last few years, but we’re happy to keep giving them the old college try. How’s the new oldest Crown Royal ever? Let’s dig in.

Crown Royal 32 Years Old Review

Going in with a fresh bottle and an open mind, the whisky certainly feels more refined and interesting this year. There is still plenty of austerity on the nose — I don’t see that going away, of course — with notes of candied orange peel, menthol, black pepper, and flowery saffron all dominant — and perhaps a bit scattered. Over time, the lattermost begins to take over, as the nose gets increasingly floral as it sits in glass. Best of all, that hoary asphalt and creosote character I’ve seen with other Crown Royal releases of this general age level is mercifully absent (or at least extremely muted).

The palate is shorter and sharper than the rather sweet nose suggests, those orange peel notes punctuated and peppery, offering something of a holiday feel. The sweetness settles down slowly as it reaches into notes of rum raisin and cinnamon toast, then gets just a bit more brooding with a gently leathery character, increasingly nutty as it develops. The finish is surprisingly clean but big with coconut and chocolate notes that seem to come from nowhere, lightly peppery on the fade-out. Definitely the best of the ultra-aged Crowns to date. (Somehow.)

92 proof.

A- / $750 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

title: Review: 2025 Bodegas Lan Verdejo
summary:

It is earnest and certain you are capable of more than you’ve been settling for, and we all could use this sort of cheerleader from time…

The post Review: 2025 Bodegas Lan Verdejo appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
The website copy on Bodegas Lan’s website reads less like a promotional vehicle for Spanish wine and more like a commercial break in between acts of a wellness podcast. It is earnest and certain you are capable of more than you’ve been settling for, and we all could use this sort of cheerleader from time to time. The navigation contains sections called “Say Yes To Yourself” and “Between You And Me.” There are pleas for you, gentle reader, to “focus on what you truly want,” to “smile at yourself,” and, most ambitiously, “allow every drop to tell its own story”. This is a curveball from the usual narratives. Wine internet is a rush-hour freeway crowded with swaths of multigenerational family stories, fervent invocations of passion, and photographs of impossibly good-looking models (possibly replicants) cradling grapes at golden hour. If Bodegas Lan has decided instead to operate as a motivational speaker with a Rioja license, the industry is all the better for it. We are, in the spirit of the occasion, saying yes.

What we are saying “yes” to specifically is this 100% Verdejo: carrying aromas of peach and lemon with a touch of rosemary as it warms in the glass. On the palate, pineapple and bergamot and a slight mineral thread of slate appear first, all organized around vibrant acidity. Grapefruit eventually appears and lingers softly, and the peach note returns on the clean and direct finish, taking things full circle.

The website recommends pairing this with “moments of fun and laughter outside in the sunshine,” which is the kind of serving suggestion that hits the bullseye or is entirely useless, depending on one’s current disposition. Sushi, it turns out, works equally well, with considerably less logistical coordination, similar levels of mirth and zero sunscreen.

B+ / $14

title: Review: Bulleit Rye 20 Years Old
summary:

The post Review: Bulleit Rye 20 Years Old appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Bulleit Rye Whiskey debuted in 2011 as a new whiskey distilled in Lawrenceburg, Indiana from the now well-known mashbill of 95% rye and 5% malted barley. Bulleit turned to Indiana-distilled rye several years before the 95/5 recipe gained widespread attention throughout the whiskey world. Marketed as “Frontier Whiskey,” Bulleit truly occupied that frontier when it came to sourcing MGP’s rye whiskey.

The brand expanded on that foundation with the release of Bulleit Rye 12 Years Old in 2019 and again in 2024. The 2024 edition included rye whiskey as old as 17 years within the blend. Then, in July 2026, as the United States marked its 250th anniversary, Nicole Austin, Diageo’s Director of American Whiskey Liquid Development and Capability, raised the bar once again with Bulleit Rye 20 Years Old, the oldest rye whiskey ever released under the Bulleit name.

Although the label makes no reference to the nation’s semiquincentennial, the release included a fitting production run of 1,776 bottles. Long before bourbon earned recognition as America’s native spirit, rye whiskey held that role. It was already part of American life in 1776 when the colonies declared independence from Great Britain, and it also stood as a patriotic alternative to the rum trade that helped finance the British Crown.

Released in July 2026, Bulleit Rye 20 Years Old arrives at a cask strength of 137 proof with an age statement of 20 years. Even that number understates what is actually in the bottle. Austin and her team initially evaluated 82 barrels before narrowing the selection to 48. By that point, evaporation had taken such a toll that several barrels were either nearly empty or completely empty.

The final blend draws from barrels filled on May 17, 2005, October 11, 2004, and April 3, 2003, all of which were dumped during the spring of 2026. While the label simply states “20 Years Old,” the whiskey itself includes components aged approximately 20 years and 10 months, 21 years and 4 months, and 22 years and 10 months.

Unlike Diageo’s Blade and Bow Bourbon 30 Years Old, the Bulleit barrels showed no signs of barrel consolidation, as fill levels varied considerably from barrel to barrel.

Every barrel spent its entire maturation inside the historic 1935-era Stitzel-Weller warehouses in Louisville, Kentucky, specifically Warehouses L, Z, and B. Warehouse Z, a metal-sided palletized warehouse, housed some barrels during their final year or so. Warehouses L and B follow the traditional Stitzel-Weller design, with each floor stacked only three barrels high. Tunnel windows, generous aisle spacing, and excellent airflow set those buildings apart.

Most of the barrels spent their lives on the first floor, while one barrel rested on the second floor. The fourth floor was the highest location represented anywhere in the blend. Within Warehouses L and B, the barrels occupied rows 17 and 27 near the outer edges of the buildings.

Austin began by marrying six barrels before making additional adjustments with other barrels until the blend reached its final composition. Once assembled, the whiskey mingled for three to four weeks before bottling.

Bulleit Rye 12 Years Old earned considerable praise, but does Bulleit Rye 20 Years Old deserve the same recognition, or perhaps even more?

New charred oak barrels paired with the American climate can make straight bourbon and straight rye whiskey increasingly difficult propositions once they reach 20 years of age and beyond. The romance of a 20-year-old rye whiskey is easy to appreciate. At the same time, it is equally plausible that the average barrel of straight rye at that age winds up tasting more like chewing on a table leg than drinking great whiskey.

Nicole Austin has built a reputation for getting the most out of mature whiskey, so the question becomes: what did she accomplish with ultra-aged rye that spent more than two decades inside the storied warehouses of Stitzel-Weller?

Bulleit Rye 20 Years Old Review

The nose opens with a bounty of dried and oxidized fruit, led by dried apricots and dehydrated apple chips. It delivers an immediate rush of concentrated fruit. As those aromas gradually recede, the signature Indiana spearmint associated with the 95/5 mashbill becomes increasingly apparent. Sarsaparilla follows before charred orange peel finally arrives late. The trademark aromas of Indiana rye remain intact, though they present with less brightness than usual after more than two decades in oak. Even at 137 proof, the nose never suggests excessive tannins.

The palate immediately announces the proof with a quick rush of ethanol before Indiana dill takes over. Grilled peaches follow, though they resemble canned peach slices cooked over charcoal more than fresh peaches, combining juicy sweetness with smoky charring. Orange marmalade transitions into sage, bringing to mind a spoonful of Kraft Stove Top Traditional Sage Stuffing Mix. The mouth-coating viscosity makes every sip stay, though the proof is substantial enough to draw a little sweat from the brow.

The proof becomes even more apparent on the finish. Cigar ash arrives first, followed by brief peppermint oil, spicy white pepper, over-toasted pecans, and finally pine resin. The finish more than anywhere else showcases the effects of extended maturation.

Nicole Austin accomplished something that becomes increasingly difficult as rye whiskey approaches and surpasses the 20-year mark. This whiskey displays its age while remaining true to its identity as rye whiskey rather than allowing oak to dominate the profile.

Bulleit Rye 20 Years Old is an outstanding bottle for special occasions, best shared with friends rather than poured casually. At 137 proof, it’s meant to savor slowly.

Its $299 price tag also prompts comparison with the 2024 edition of Bulleit Rye 12 Years Old. That release included whiskey up to 17 years old and retailed for $55. The jump from 92 proof to 137 proof certainly changes the experience, yet the 2024 Bulleit Rye 12 Years Old remains an exceptional whiskey and an excellent everyday pour.

For anyone comfortable spending $299 on a bottle, Bulleit Rye 20 Years Old earns a place on the shelf. Those who are not can confidently choose the 2024 Bulleit Rye 12 Years Old at a fraction of the price.

137 proof.

A / $299

The post Review: Teremana Tequila, Complete Lineup (Updated 2026) appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
2020 saw a raft of celebrity-branded wines and spirits, but none was arguably bigger than Teremana, which is backed by Dwayne “The Rock” Johnson. Teremana is a pot-distilled tequila made with 100% Highlands agave. It’s currently available in blanco, reposado, and anejo expressions.

We received all three (eventually) for review. Below you’ll find our original coverage of the blanco and reposado releases from 2020, and 2026 updates for all three expressions.

All are 80 proof (and also available in both 750ml and 1 liter formats). NOM 1613.

Teremana Tequila Blanco (2020) Review

The nose here is immediately a bit plain — vegetal, muddy, and a bit sweaty, though it’s at least short of off-putting. The palate opens up a bit, initially showing notes of white pepper and some lemon. There’s a gentle sweetness rolling through the body, but a funky, heavily earthy note — not really like agave but more like damp dirt — is never far away, invariably rushing back to meet you. The pungent nose is hard to shake throughout, eventually settling into a note more akin to green beans than fresh agave, muddying the entire experience. This is usable as a mixer only. C / $30 [BUY IT NOW FROM TOTAL WINE] [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

Teremana Tequila Blanco (2026) Review

Almost six years later, this tequila hasn’t changed appreciably, but it has at least improved. While the nose remains rather simple, it’s not nearly as muddy or pungent as we originally experienced. A big note of roasted agave and subtle undertones of stewed green bell pepper make for a monotone bouquet, but there’s an inviting balance of sweetness. On the palate, that measured sweetness remains the highlight with the agave still presenting an overly earthy character that dulls its complexity and amplifies the ethanol. A bit of black pepper and lemon oil on the midpalate adds some depth, but the finish is muddled with a mix of bright, nondescript citrus and green notes that once again tend more toward canned vegetables than agave. Improved since our first outing but still just mixing material. -DB B- [BUY IT NOW FROM TOTAL WINE] [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

Teremana Tequila Reposado (2020) Review

Oddly, no aging information is provided, though we do know the spirit is rested in ex-bourbon barrels. Reposados usually find their aromatics tempered by barrel time, but this expression doesn’t let up on that funky, vegetal nose, though here more of a black pepper note comes through. The palate does show some of the sweetness one expects from a reposado, but not an overwhelming amount. Still, it’s enough to temper the heavy earthiness that the blanco shows, and as it develops in the glass, some butterscotch and lemon elements begin to dominate, giving the finish more of a welcome approachability. B- / $33 [BUY IT NOW FROM TOTAL WINE] [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

Teremana Tequila Reposado (2026) Review

There is still no specific aging information for this reposado. Conjecture on the internet seems to coalesce around the two-month minimum, which I tend to suspect given the color. The aroma is once again improved in this revisit with that vegetal funk subdued by the oak and complementing the cooked agave notes with a balanced layer of light brown sugar and butterscotch. Notes of white pepper and subtle lime zest add a bit of energy to what is an otherwise simple but pleasant aroma. As with our first taste, the palate shows a measured, wood-driven sweetness, not nearly the syrupy sweet character of some other reposados. And while restrained, it still manages to soften some of the earthier edges of the blanco with silky caramelized sugars and hints of citrus, building into a warm finish that lingers with a little cracked pepper and agave syrup. Not quite enough depth for sipping, but an elevated cocktail option over the blanco. -DB B [BUY IT NOW FROM TOTAL WINE] [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

Teremana Tequila Anejo (2026) Review

Even though Teremana’s anejo expression launched at the end of 2021, it took us a little while (OK, a long while) to run down a sample. Like the reposado, we don’t get any specific details on the maturation but again judging from the color I would venture somewhere close to the 12-month minimum. The barrel notes on the nose are not appreciably different from the reposado, but they dominate even more the earthy agave that should be somewhere underneath it all. Notes of toffee, vanilla buttercream, Demerara sugar, and a touch of coffee bean all show, once again, a welcome, balanced sweetness, but aside from undertones of agave syrup, there’s not much more than oak in the mix. The palate adds bigger butterscotch flavors than the reposado, but it somehow comes across a bit thinner. Hints of lime peel and agave add some complexity before washing out into a gentle, medium-length finish of vanilla icing and white pepper. Exceedingly approachable, it’s the best sipper of the trio, but the reposado is more interesting. -DB B / $40 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

The post Review: 2024 Ridge Vineyards Grenache Blanc Paso Robles appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
While people may try in earnest, no one in Kentucky can really pinpoint with certitude the end of the summer season and the beginning of autumn. The people who do often gesture vaguely to the arrival of pumpkin spice and Keeneland. Under no circumstances should their opinions carry any weight. Thankfully for those who don’t even bother to partake in this exercise, this Grenache Blanc from Ridge Vineyards shows up in a quantum state of living both seasons at once. Kind of like a guy wearing cargo shorts, an undersized soccer jersey picked up on clearance and sandals to Christmas dinner, oblivious to the world around him.

It’s a blend of 85% Grenache Blanc, 12% Picpoul, and 3% Roussanne and presents with aromas of pear, orange zest and mild jasmine. However, it’s on the palate where this wine spreads out with ample generosity: plenty of pear joined by ripe apricot, hazelnut, and a big current of minerality on the finish with enough acidity to keep things well focused throughout.

What you end up with is a wine built for the tail end of a long patio dinner, and it’s the first evening you notice you needed a sweatshirt or sweater and failed to bring one along. It doesn’t rush things, and when it comes to enjoying this bottle, nor should you. It already knows where the calendar is going and works well in either season with measured restraint and class.

A- / $43

title: Review: Shang Whiskey Dan Ya and East + West Kentucky Blend

The post Review: Shang Whiskey Dan Ya and East + West Kentucky Blend appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
It’s not every day we get to sample an entirely new category of spirits. But that’s very much what Shang Whiskey is selling, with two launch offerings built around a whiskey distilled from Chinese baijiu.

The first — Dàn Ya — is redistilled from sauce-aroma (jiàngxiang) baijiu, which is produced from red sorghum. The redistilled spirit is then sent to Kentucky, where it is aged for under a year in American oak. It’s a fusion of Chinese and American production techniques, original enough that Shang is promoting it as a new category unto itself: jiàngxiang whiskey.

Shang’s second expression — the East + West Kentucky Blend — begins with the same jiàngxiang whiskey base. It’s blended with a Kentucky-distilled red sorghum whiskey, then aged in American oak before bottling.

Almost as notable as the production methods are the array of players involved in bringing the new spirits to market. Shang is owned by Maritine Brands, itself a joint venture between True Essence Foods and Guìzhou Guótái Shùzhì Liquor Group. Further partners include Whiskey House of Kentucky (in Elizabethtown) and The Blending House (in Shelbyville).

It’s a unique approach to melding distinct spirits categories and styles. And while many Westerners are still unfamiliar with baijiu, it’s generally considered the world’s largest spirits category, with annual sales almost double that of the global whiskey market. At the outset, Shang seems keen on targeting two separate consumer bases: baijiu-curious Americans, and existing baijiu drinkers searching for an injection of novelty.

Let’s dive in.

Shang Whiskey Dàn Ya Review

The baijiu used for Dàn Ya’s jiàngxiang whiskey begins with red sorghum in the Chìshui River basin. The sorghum base undergoes solid-state fermentation using dàqu, a starter that facilitates both saccharification and fermentation. Production follows a complex series of eight fermentations, separated by seven distillations. The distillate is rested in oxygen permeable clay pots for a minimum of three years. Finally, the baijiu is pot distilled and pressure filtered before shipping to Kentucky, where the resulting jiàngxiang whiskey is aged in American oak for between one month to “just under” a year.

On the nose, dedicated whiskey drinkers will likely encounter something quite new. Early aromas are at once tangy, sour, fruity, floral, and salty, somewhere between overripe tropical fruit and a savory fermented sauce or bean paste. Additional notes include bitter melon, lemongrass, pickled watermelon rind, and unsweetened chocolate. It’s certainly a broad mix, and it takes time to really parse the individual components. Oak develops later on, lending touches of vanilla and light caramel, which (eventually) push the nose into more familiar whiskey territory.

The palate starts with floral simple syrup and a big hit of red peppercorns, the latter dominating for a couple sips. After some acclimation comes loads more fruit, including tart berry compote, passionfruit, lychee, and pomelo. The back palate brings salinity and sweet/savory red bean paste, with lingering pepper. 100 proof.

B+ / $65 (500ml)

Shang Whiskey East + West Kentucky Blend Review

East + West starts with the jiàngxiang whiskey base and marries it with whiskey distilled from 100% red sorghum. That second component is produced at Whiskey House via sweet mash fermentation and grain-on column distillation up to 155 proof. (A Whiskey House representative confirmed the team used a relatively neutral yeast and enzymes similar to a high corn bourbon.) After the two components are blended, they undergo maturation in American oak barrels.

East + West kicks off with a profile far more familiar to whiskey drinkers. The nose begins with toasted oak and fermenting grain, and at first, it’s a little reminiscent of fermenting mash. Baking spice and chocolate are up next, and once again, it’s still firmly in whiskey territory: allspice, clove, and nutmeg meet hot cocoa. Eventually, some of the funky, ripe fruit character from Dàn Ya rolls in, along with a savory, peppery sauce (hoisin comes to mind).

The palate borrows a lot from Dàn Ya, with both pepper and tart fruit dialed back by around half. That allows for more caramel and milk chocolate, along with threads of bright red cherry and honeydew I didn’t pick up on the first expression. Similarly, the saline is toned down, and in its place we’ve got both pickled and candied ginger. The sweeter finish brings golden raisins and black pepper.

For American palates, East + West is less adventurous but more familiar. My guess is that could up the appeal stateside, though it reigns in some of what makes Dàn Ya intricate and fun. 92 proof.

B+ / $46 (500ml)
